outcome: No accepted resolution as of 11 Oct 2026: the infinitude of cousin primes (p and p+4 both prime) is open as far as the sources show. Since 26 Jan 2024 the only results that address this exact question are unrefereed claims (a restricted Zenodo preprint from 29 Jan 2026 asserting it, and general-Polignac claims from Jan 2026, Jun 2026 and 2025 that would settle it if valid). Separately, bounded-gap progress on the smallest gap H₁ moved sharply in Aug–Sep 2026 (H₁ ≤ 240, 236, 212, 186), but none of it singles out gap 4.
problem_asks: One question: are there infinitely many primes p such that p+4 is also prime (infinitely many cousin prime pairs (p, p+4))? Nothing is asked about density, a bound, or a particular size. Wikipedia's Polignac's conjecture article states the same claim for n = 4 ('For n = 4, it says there are infinitely many cousin primes (p, p + 4)'). The Hardy–Littlewood density claim (cousin and twin primes share an asymptotic density) is not in the bullet and is recorded only as context.

events.what_happened: Shouyu Du and Zhanle Du posted 'There are infinitely many cousin primes' (arXiv math/0510329, 16 Oct 2005; v2 24 Oct 2005). The abstract reads 'We proved that there are infinitely many cousin primes.' Comments: '16 pages, 1 figure'. The arXiv page shows no journal reference and no withdrawal notice.
events.revisions: v1 16 Oct 2005; v2 24 Oct 2005 (no change note on the abstract page).
events.delivers: Claims the whole bullet: infinitely many primes p with p+4 prime. Its scope matches the bullet exactly, so if the argument were valid it would resolve the problem.
events.remains: Nothing, if the argument is valid. I found no one who has assessed its validity.
events.doubts: I read the paper only through an ar5iv rendering that a tool summarised; I did not check the argument myself. Per that summary, the proof is a contradiction argument (Section 6, eqs. 6.2 to 6.8) that rests on a lower bound (Lemma 6.1) built from a sieve lemma (Lemma 4.2). Section 5, which justifies Lemma 4.2, is described as 'largely heuristic' (it calls a sequence 'an effective nature sequence'). Lemma 4.4's inequality is said to be 'asserted rather than shown' ('before deleting the multiples of other primes'). Identifying sieve survivors with primes depends on a D₁ correction that the paper argues for. None of this has been answered in print that I could find.
events.direction: Affirmative: asserts that the set of cousin primes is infinite.

events.what_happened: Shan-Guang Tan, 'On the solution of the Collatz problem' (arXiv 1110.3465), v1 16 Oct 2011, current v32 29 Dec 2025. The abstract is about the Collatz problem and claims that 'the Collatz problem is solved'. The abstract does not mention cousin primes. A search snippet listed a 'Theorem of cousin primes' section and a 'Lemma 20.2' in this paper, and a search summary called that lemma circular. I could not read the PDF, so neither point is verified.
events.revisions: v1 16 Oct 2011; ... v32 29 Dec 2025 (per arXiv listing; intermediate versions not checked).
events.delivers: Claims the Collatz conjecture, which is not this problem. Whether it contains a valid cousin-prime theorem is unknown to me; the abstract does not claim one.
events.remains: All of problem_asks, unless the unverified section is a valid proof.
events.doubts: Claims a solution to Collatz, a famous problem, in a paper revised 32 times; the cousin-prime section is seen only in a search snippet and could not be read.
events.direction: Affirmative for Collatz (a different problem). Cousin-prime content: unknown.

events.what_happened: H. J. Weber, 'A Sieve for Cousin Primes' (arXiv 1204.3795), v1 17 Apr 2012, v2 24 Apr 2012. The abstract says a sieve is constructed for primes of the form 3(2m+1)±2 ('twin primes at distance 4') and that 'the asymptotic law of its main term has the expected form and magnitude of its coefficient'. It does not claim that infinitely many cousin primes exist.
events.revisions: v1 17 Apr 2012; v2 24 Apr 2012 (comment: 'A clarification added to, a misstatement removed from introduction').
events.delivers: A sieve construction and an asymptotic claim for the main term of a count of ranks. It does not establish infinitude, and the abstract does not say whether the asymptotic is unconditional.
events.remains: All of problem_asks.
events.doubts: Only the abstract was read. The abstract's sieve is for 'twin primes at distance 4' while the title says 'cousin primes', which is the same pair pattern.
events.direction: Neutral: a sieve/asymptotic result that stops short of infinitude.

events.what_happened: Yitang Zhang, 'Bounded gaps between primes' (Annals of Mathematics). Received 17 Apr 2013, accepted 21 May 2013; published vol. 179 no. 3 (2014). Abstract: 'It is proved that liminf (p_{n+1} − p_n) < 7×10⁷.' I found no arXiv preprint. A Quanta report followed on 19 May 2013 (per search results, not opened).
events.delivers: Some even gap below 7×10⁷ occurs infinitely often between consecutive primes. It does not say which gap, so it does not establish that gap 4 recurs infinitely often.
events.remains: All of problem_asks: the difference 4 is not singled out.

checked_by.qualification: Journal of record for research mathematics.
checked_by.what_they_did: Accepted the manuscript (accepted 21 May 2013) and published it (vol. 179 no. 3, 2014).

events.direction: Toward bounded gaps: H₁ is finite. Neutral for the gap-4 question.

events.what_happened: Janos Pintz, 'Polignac Numbers, Conjectures of Erdős on Gaps between Primes, Arithmetic Progressions in Primes, and the Bounded Gap Conjecture' (arXiv 1305.6289, 27 May 2013). The abstract I read says only that the paper 'prove[s] a number of surprising results about gaps between consecutive primes'. Its specific claims come from secondary sources: a CORDIS project report and a 2015 arXiv note by Stijn Hanson (arXiv 1501.06690, search snippet only). Per those, Pintz showed there are infinitely many Polignac numbers (even integers that occur as infinitely many consecutive-prime differences), that they have positive lower density, and that consecutive Polignac numbers differ by a uniformly bounded amount.
events.delivers: If the secondary descriptions are right: infinitely many even numbers are Polignac numbers, with positive lower density among even numbers. That does not say the number 4 is one, and a density statement about a set of even numbers does not single out 4.
events.remains: Whether 4 is a Polignac number, which is the cousin question. Also the twin case and the general Polignac conjecture.
events.doubts: I did not read the body. Strong and weak Polignac numbers are distinguished in secondary summaries, and the constant 1/354 comes from a lecture slide. The only later engagement I found is Hanson's note, which cites the result and gives conditional bounds; it is not an independent check.
events.direction: Toward Polignac-type statements; does not single out gap 4.

events.what_happened: James Maynard, 'Small gaps between primes' (arXiv 1311.4600), first submitted 19 Nov 2013. The abstract gives the unconditional bound liminf (p_{n+1} − p_n) ≤ 600, the bound ≤ 12 under the Elliott–Halberstam conjecture, and that the prime k-tuples conjecture holds for a positive proportion of admissible k-tuples for each k, with the consequence that liminf (p_{n+m} − p_n) is finite for every m.
events.delivers: Unconditionally: some even gap ≤ 600 recurs infinitely often. The admissible-tuple result gives, for large k, a positive proportion of admissible k-tuples containing at least two primes infinitely often. Neither says the specific pattern {0, 4} (a pair differing by 4) is prime infinitely often.
events.remains: Whether the difference 4 recurs infinitely often, and the twin case H₁ = 2.

checked_by.qualification: Journal of record for research mathematics.
checked_by.what_they_did: Published the paper (Annals 181 no. 1, 2015), per a search listing; I did not open that page.

events.direction: Toward bounded gaps: H₁ ≤ 600 unconditionally. Neutral for gap 4.

events.what_happened: D.H.J. Polymath, 'Variants of the Selberg sieve, and bounded intervals containing many primes' (arXiv 1407.4897), first submitted 18 Jul 2014, v4 22 Dec 2014. The abstract gives H₁ ≤ 246 unconditionally and H₁ ≤ 6 under the generalized Elliott–Halberstam conjecture. The project retrospective is arXiv 1409.8361 (30 Sep 2014), which does not mention cousin primes.
events.revisions: v2 2 Aug 2014; v3 3 Sep 2014; v4 22 Dec 2014 (per arXiv abstract page).
events.delivers: Unconditionally: some even gap ≤ 246 recurs infinitely often, not specified. Conditionally on generalized EH: H₁ ≤ 6, so one of the gaps 2, 4 or 6 recurs infinitely often. That does not single out 4. (A search summary called this 'gap 6 infinitely often'; that overstates it.)
events.remains: Whether the difference 4 recurs infinitely often, and the twin case.

checked_by.who: The Polymath collaboration (participants named in the retrospective, arXiv 1409.8361)
checked_by.qualification: Participants in an open, online, collaborative verification of the sieve argument.
checked_by.what_they_did: Collaborative online checking and refinement of the argument, reported in the retrospective. A later Cambridge volume collects the results per a search listing (not opened).

events.direction: Toward bounded gaps: H₁ ≤ 246 unconditionally. Neutral for gap 4.

events.what_happened: Theophilus Agama, 'A proof of the twin prime conjecture' (arXiv 1707.03265). The abstract claims a lower bound (1+o(1))·x/(2𝒞 log²x) for the number of primes p ≤ x with p+2 also prime, and says this 'implies' infinitely many twin primes. The v4 revision (8 Mar 2026) says the paper was reformatted and the introduction expanded and that 'the ideas remain unchanged'. The abstract does not mention cousin primes.
events.revisions: v2 28 Jul 2021; v3 4 Mar 2022; v4 8 Mar 2026 (reformatted, introduction expanded, 'the ideas remain unchanged').
events.delivers: Claims the twin case (difference 2). That is a different question from the difference 4, so it does not settle the bullet.
events.remains: All of problem_asks: the cousin question is not addressed.
events.doubts: No refereeing; the same ideas are carried into a 2026 revision. I read only the abstract.
events.direction: Affirmative for twin primes (a neighbouring problem). Silent on cousin primes.

events.what_happened: Marko V. Jankovic, 'Proof of the Twin Prime Conjecture (Together with the Proof of Polignac's Conjecture for Cousin Primes)' (arXiv 1903.05410, math.GM). The abstract says 'The same approach is used to prove the Polignac's conjecture for cousin primes.' The paper has 15 versions, 13 Mar 2019 to 2 Jun 2022, no comments and no journal reference.
events.delivers: Claims the cousin case (the n = 4 case of Polignac) and the twin case. If valid, the scope matches the bullet exactly.
events.remains: Nothing, if valid. Its validity is unassessed.
events.doubts: Posted to math.GM; fifteen revisions with no journal reference or recorded engagement. I read the abstract and listing only, not the body, so I cannot say what the key step is. The claim covers two famous problems at once.
events.direction: Affirmative: asserts infinitude for the n = 4 case.

events.what_happened: Mbakiso F. Mothebe, Dintle N. Kagiso and Ben T. Modise, 'A proof of cases of de Polignac's conjecture' (arXiv 1912.09290). The abstract says the paper 'proves the well known twin prime conjecture as well as several cases of Alphonse de Polignac's conjecture'. It names no gap. Comment: an arXiv admin note records substantial text overlap with arXiv:1909.02205.
events.revisions: v2 10 Jan 2020; v3 18 Jun 2020; v4 19 Aug 2020; v5 30 Jan 2024; v6 26 Jul 2024 (the version shown).
events.delivers: Claims the twin case and 'several cases' of Polignac, without naming them. Gap 4 is not named, so the abstract neither clearly covers nor clearly excludes the cousin question.
events.remains: Whether 4 is among the unnamed 'several cases'; the full Polignac conjecture.
events.doubts: The abstract names no gap; the arXiv admin note records text overlap with another arXiv paper; I did not read the body. The 2024 revisions are after the frozen date but do not change the first date.
events.direction: Affirmative for the twin case and for unnamed Polignac cases. Gap 4 not specified.

events.what_happened: John K. Sellers, 'A step towards proving de Polignac's Conjecture' (arXiv 2108.13834), v1 27 Aug 2021, v4 16 Nov 2021. The abstract says it is a conditional proof of de Polignac's conjecture 'for a range of known gaps', and that 'the full conjecture requires additional proof that such number pairs exist for all even gaps'. It does not name the gaps.
events.revisions: v2 13 Sep 2021; v3 13 Nov 2021; v4 16 Nov 2021 (comment: adds a section that 'proves the existence of some gaps').
events.delivers: Conditional on a hypothesis the abstract I read does not state, it establishes infinitely many prime pairs with the given gap for an unnamed range of gaps. Whether 4 is in that range is not stated.
events.remains: The full Polignac conjecture, including n = 4 unless 4 is in the unnamed range.
events.doubts: Self-described as conditional; the condition is not visible on the abstract page; no journal reference.
events.direction: Toward de Polignac, conditionally; does not specify gap 4.

events.what_happened: Jason R. South, 'An Algebraic Approach to the Goldbach Conjecture' (arXiv 2206.01179), v1 31 May 2022, last revised 9 Sep 2026 (v16). The current abstract claims 'We prove the Goldbach Conjecture using p-adic analysis and algebraic methods' and does not mention Polignac. A search summary said an earlier version also claimed Polignac; I did not confirm that.
events.delivers: A Goldbach claim, which is a different problem. The current abstract says nothing about gap 4.
events.remains: All of problem_asks.
events.doubts: A claimed proof of Goldbach with no referee found; the comment says 'significant simplifications' were made in the latest version. I read only the abstract and listing.
events.direction: Affirmative for Goldbach (a different problem). Silent on gap 4 in the current abstract.

events.what_happened: Daniele Bufalo, Michele Bufalo and Felice Iavernaro, 'A probabilistic approach to the twin prime and cousin prime conjectures' (arXiv 2303.17998), submitted 31 Mar 2023. The abstract, per a tool summary, shows that the probability that a prime-square interval contains a twin pair and a cousin pair tends to 1, and proposes 'a new, more stringent conjecture' about infinitely many twin and cousin primes. It does not claim to prove the cousin conjecture.
events.delivers: A heuristic: a probabilistic limit about intervals between prime squares, plus a proposed conjecture. It does not establish infinitude of cousin primes.
events.remains: All of problem_asks.
events.doubts: I read the abstract summary only, not the body (20 pages).
events.direction: Heuristic support for infinitude; not a proof either way.

events.what_happened: Daniel Sankei, Loyford Njagi and Josephine Mutembei, 'A logical proof of the Polignac's conjecture based on partitions of an even number of a new formulation', Meru University MUSTIC conference proceedings (3rd MUSTIC, 2024 volume), article published 10 Apr 2025. The abstract says both that 'Polignac's Conjecture remains unproven' and that 'a logical proof of the Polignac's Conjecture is provided'. The gap variable is missing from the abstract text as extracted. It mentions only the twin case.
events.delivers: Claims the general Polignac conjecture, which would include n = 4 (cousin primes) if valid. The abstract contradicts itself on whether the conjecture is proved.
events.remains: Nothing, if valid. Its validity is unassessed.
events.doubts: Self-contradictory abstract ('remains unproven' versus 'a logical proof ... is provided'); the gap variable is missing from the extracted text; the PDF is unreadable to my tool, so I could not check the argument. The review process of the proceedings is not stated on the page I read.
events.direction: Affirmative for general Polignac (which covers n = 4).

events.what_happened: Brendan Lynch, 'Unconditional Analytical Closure of Polignac's Conjecture via UFT-F Spectral Invariance' (Zenodo 18369489, DOI 10.5281/zenodo.18369489), v1 25 Jan 2026, CC BY 4.0. The abstract says 'This work presents the unconditional analytical closure of Polignac's Conjecture.' The record lists two companion Zenodo records (10.5281/zenodo.17566371 and 10.5281/zenodo.17622862) as supplements, which I did not open.
events.delivers: Claims Polignac for all even gaps, which would include n = 4 if valid. Per the page summary, gap 4 is supported only computationally ('tested gaps'; 'the strongest computational base case to date'), and the error-term estimate is stated under RH, which sits uneasily with 'unconditional'.
events.remains: The cousin question is settled only if the general claim is valid; the page's own gap-4 support is computational.
events.doubts: (a) 'Unconditional' in title and abstract versus an error-term estimate stated under RH (per the tool's reading of the page). (b) Gap 4 supported only computationally, per the page. (c) A search summary reports numerical checks up to N = 10⁹; I did not verify that. (d) No institutional affiliation. (e) The companion records are unopened. I read the landing page, not the full PDF.
events.direction: Affirmative for general Polignac, which would include gap 4.

events.what_happened: Jorge Zafaranich and Daniel Augusto (listed as an independent researcher in Argentina), 'Cousin Primes as a Persistence Phenomenon in a Canonically Indexed Sieve' (Zenodo 18410998), v1 29 Jan 2026. The abstract says 'infinitely many cousin prime pairs exist' and that 'All arguments are exact, finite, and deterministic.' The files are restricted and need a login.
events.delivers: Claims the full bullet: infinitely many primes p with p+4 prime. The scope matches exactly, so if valid it resolves the problem.
events.remains: Nothing, if valid. Validity unassessed because the full text is restricted.
events.doubts: Restricted full text, so I could not check the argument; only the abstract page was read. A search-result summary (not the file) describes the central step as an 'Archimedean non-coverage principle' that the abstract asserts; I could not confirm that. Self-deposited by an author with no institutional affiliation shown; no journal.
events.direction: Affirmative: asserts that the set of cousin primes is infinite.

events.what_happened: 'A Proof of Polignac's Conjecture via Translational Tower Sieve and Precise Cutting' (Zenodo 20758563, CC BY 4.0, resource type 'Dataset'), published 19 Jun 2026. Metadata lists three people with roles 'Annotator' and 'Data manager' and no affiliations. The abstract says 'Iteration gives the lower bound N_t ≫ t², hence N_t → ∞, proving the Polignac Conjecture', and describes the argument as 'elementary number theory'. The page shows version v11 and a newer version. A search summary says a 24 Jun 2026 version (v12) is retitled 'Fixed-Window Tower Sieve with Precision Period Cutting' and ends by applying Mertens' theorem; I did not open that version.
events.revisions: v11 (19 Jun 2026) per the page; a newer version exists (per a search summary, v12 dated 24 Jun 2026, retitled).
events.delivers: Claims Polignac for all even gaps, which would include n = 4 if valid. The page does not say whether gap 4 is treated separately.
events.remains: Nothing, if valid. Validity unassessed.
events.doubts: Metadata roles are unusual and no affiliations are given; the record is a self-deposited 'Dataset'; the title changed in a later version (per summary); it claims an elementary proof of a famous open problem. I did not read the body.
events.direction: Affirmative for general Polignac, which would include gap 4.

events.what_happened: Axiom Math's Lean formalization of the H₁ ≤ 246 theorem ('BGP246'; project page primegaps.axiommath.ai, library PrimeGapsLib), reported as published as an interactive blueprint on 17 Aug 2026 (per secondary reports; I could not read the blueprint PDF). The project page says it formalizes 'the Maynard argument in detail, but only the portion of Polymath8b used for the bound 246', and that AxiomProver 'produced machine-checkable Lean 4 proofs built on Mathlib and Kontorovich and Tao's PrimeNumberTheoremAnd'. The formalization assumes the Bombieri–Vinogradov theorem.
events.delivers: A machine-checked version of H₁ ≤ 246 relative to Bombieri–Vinogradov. It formalizes an existing 2014 human result and establishes no new statement. It concerns bounded gaps, not the difference 4.
events.remains: All of problem_asks.
events.doubts: Whether the Lean statement faithfully captures H₁ ≤ 246 was not checked by anyone outside the project. Sorry-freeness is not stated on the page I read. Contributor counts differ by source (seven named authors in the blueprint per a search summary, versus '41 named contributors' in news coverage).
events.direction: Confirms formally an existing bound (H₁ ≤ 246). No bearing on gap 4.
people: Edison Xie (named per a search summary of the blueprint)

events.what_happened: Julia Stadlmann, 'Bounded gaps between primes' (arXiv 2608.31126, math.NT), one version submitted 31 Aug 2026. The abstract says Bombieri–Vinogradov combined with newer equidistribution estimates for smooth moduli gives H₁ ≤ 240. The HTML rendering (first ~100k characters, then a further portion) states Theorem 1 with a typo ('H_m ≤ 240'), describes an exact integral computation by matrix multiplication (section 1.1) that 'can still take days', and contains no acknowledgement or AI statement in the parts I read. Science News dates the result to 'early summer 2026', which conflicts with the arXiv date.
events.delivers: H₁ ≤ 240: some even gap ≤ 240 recurs infinitely often. Not gap 4 specifically. Explicitly about the liminf of consecutive-prime gaps.
events.remains: All of problem_asks, including the twin case.
events.doubts: A new preprint with no referee found. The 240 bound depends on an exact computation over a 49-variable integral that I did not verify. The Science News timeline conflicts with the arXiv date.
events.direction: Toward bounded gaps. Neutral for gap 4.

events.what_happened: François Charton, Letong Hong, Kenny Lau, Ken Ono, Guillaume Remy, Ho Chung Siu, Ashvin A. Swaminathan, Jesse Thorner and Yunzhou Xie, 'A New Bound for Small Gaps Between Primes', hosted at primegaps.axiommath.ai/bgp212.pdf (46 pages). It is not on arXiv as far as I could find. Per search-result excerpts of the paper, it proves liminf (p_{n+1} − p_n) ≤ 212, building on Stadlmann's methods; the excerpts say the analytic ideas of Theorem 1.1 originated with Stadlmann and that the optimisation used numerical experiments on a distributed computing cluster. The PDF was unreadable to my tool, so these come from excerpts and aggregators.
events.delivers: Per the excerpts: H₁ ≤ 212, so some even gap ≤ 212 recurs infinitely often. Not gap 4 specifically.
events.remains: All of problem_asks.
events.doubts: Hosted by a company rather than an arXiv listing; my tool could not read the PDF. The statement that AxiomProver formally verified the result comes from a social-media post that an aggregator reported; I did not open either. The 212 bound was superseded in the same week by the 186 claim (below) according to secondary reports.
events.direction: Toward bounded gaps. Neutral for gap 4.

events.what_happened: OpenAI, 'Improved Short Gaps Between Primes' (cdn.openai.com PDF; the paper is dated 30 Aug 2026 per the Breakthrough Tracker and was publicly announced with GPT-6 Astra on 3 Sep 2026). Claims liminf (p_{n+1} − p_n) ≤ 186 by deriving DHL[40,2] (for an admissible 40-tuple of diameter 186, at least two primes occur infinitely often), combining equidistribution estimates from Polymath 8a and Stadlmann with 'complementary factorization conditions'. The GitHub repository openai/PrimeGaps186 (Apache-2.0) has a README that says 'The Lean results remain conditional on three explicit input axioms' and that the numerical certificate 'does not discharge any Lean axiom'. It says the build 'passed without errors or warnings', with six permitted axioms in total. It states no sorry count. A GitHub-issue summary lists the three axioms as two Kloosterman-type estimates (cited to Deligne/Katz and to Fouvry–Kowalski–Michel) and numerical integral bounds checked by a Python/FLINT certificate. The primary OpenAI page returned HTTP 403 and the PDF is unreadable to my tool.
events.revisions: Paper dated 30 Aug 2026 per the tracker; announced 3 Sep 2026. Repository has one commit with no visible date.
events.delivers: If valid, some pair of consecutive-prime gaps ≤ 186 recurs infinitely often (H₁ ≤ 186). Conditional on the three input axioms. The DHL[40,2] route gives infinitely many 40-tuples with two primes, not the specific pattern {0, 4}, so it does not settle the cousin question.
events.remains: All of problem_asks. The three input axioms remain unproven in Lean.
events.doubts: (1) The Lean results are conditional on three explicit input axioms that the README says are not proven in Lean. (2) The numerical certificate lies outside Lean. (3) The Breakthrough Tracker says 'no independent human semantic review was located'. (4) A Hacker News comment, cited secondhand, notes a roughly 10 MB Lean file with little review. (5) A priority dispute with Stadlmann (see disputes). The tracker calls it an unreviewed preprint.
events.direction: Toward bounded gaps (H₁ ≤ 186, conditional). Neutral for gap 4.
people: OpenAI (sole institution listed; no human author names in the tracker record or README)

systems.name: GPT-6 Astra
systems.what_it_did: Credited with the proof of H₁ ≤ 186. Per the tracker, the paper 'attributes the proof to GPT-6 Astra'. The GitHub README names no model. The authors' own statement was not read: the OpenAI announcement returned HTTP 403 and the PDF is binary to my tool. The name is the one given by the tracker, Science News and the GitHub-issue summary.
systems.basis_quote: The paper attributes the proof to GPT-6 Astra.

events.what_happened: Zhao Song and Song Yue, 'Bounded Gaps Between Primes: An Upper Bound of 236', IACR ePrint 2026/1893 (received 4 Sep 2026, approved 9 Sep 2026). The paper claims H₁ ≤ 236 and cites Stadlmann [Sta26] for 240. It mentions the twin prime conjecture as H₁ = 2. The ePrint page lists Song Yue at Northeastern University.
events.delivers: H₁ ≤ 236: some even gap ≤ 236 recurs infinitely often. Not gap 4 specifically.
events.remains: All of problem_asks, including the twin case.
events.doubts: A cryptology-archive preprint, not peer reviewed; 'approved' is the archive's posting step, not refereeing. The PDF was not readable (HTTP 403). It was superseded by the 186 result a few days later (per secondary reports).
events.direction: Toward bounded gaps. Neutral for gap 4.

disputes.summary: OpenAI's 186 result and Stadlmann's 240 result concern the same problem. Science News (11 Sep 2026) reports that many mathematicians were upset that OpenAI worked on the same problem without informing Stadlmann; Granville is quoted that OpenAI did not 'carefully consider' how Stadlmann was treated. OpenAI says it was in touch with Maynard but did not contact Stadlmann directly. Stadlmann says she does not feel mistreated. A German report (per a search result, unverified) says OpenAI published a 240 proof on 2 Sep 2026 without referring to Stadlmann.

Model naming conflicts across sources. Tracker, Science News and the GitHub-issue summary say 'GPT-6 Astra'. A search summary reports that a Wikipedia article on Cramér's conjecture credits 'OpenAI model GPT-5.6 Sol' with a stronger prime-gap bound. I did not open that article, so this is recorded, not resolved.
Axiom's 246 formalization credits differ: news coverage cites 41 named contributors, while the blueprint (per a search summary, not read) lists seven authors. These may be different credit lists.

The date of Stadlmann's 240 result conflicts: Science News says 'early summer 2026', and the arXiv record shows a single version dated 31 Aug 2026. I have used the arXiv date, since it is the first public written argument that I could find.

summary: No event I found settles whether there are infinitely many cousin primes; none is accepted, and as of 11 Oct 2026 the problem reads as open. The searches (33 web searches, plus opening about 35 sources, of which several PDFs were unreadable to my tool) turned up four groups. (1) Claims that address this exact question and are unrefereed: Du and Du (2005, read through a summarised ar5iv rendering, whose Section 5 is described as largely heuristic); Jankovic (2019, abstract only); Zafaranich and Augusto (Jan 2026, restricted Zenodo, abstract only). (2) General-Polignac claims that would include n = 4 if valid: Mothebe et al. (2019, names the twin case and unnamed 'several cases'); Lynch (25 Jan 2026, whose own page supports gap 4 only computationally and places an error-term estimate under RH while calling itself unconditional); a Zenodo tower-sieve proof (19 Jun 2026, with odd metadata roles and a later retitled version per a search summary, not opened); and a 2025 Kenyan conference paper whose abstract both says Polignac 'remains unproven' and that a logical proof 'is provided'. None of these has been engaged with publicly that I could find, and the only older engagement is Hanson's note on Pintz's density result. (3) Conditional or partial results that do not single out 4: Sellers (2021), and Pintz (2013), whose 'Polignac numbers' result is known to me only through secondary sources. (4) Bounded-gap progress on H₁ (the smallest gap that recurs infinitely often): Zhang (2013), Maynard (2013), Polymath (2014, unconditional 246, and conditional H₁ ≤ 6), Stadlmann (31 Aug 2026, H₁ ≤ 240), Song and Yue (9 Sep 2026, H₁ ≤ 236), Charton et al. (Sep 2026, H₁ ≤ 212, with its PDF unreadable to my tool), and OpenAI (announced 3 Sep 2026, H₁ ≤ 186, credited to 'GPT-6 Astra' and conditional on three input axioms). Group (4) is the AI-relevant cluster, but it concerns a neighbouring question: H₁ ≤ c says that some gap ≤ c recurs infinitely often, not that the gap 4 does, so I judge it not to bear on this bullet. Axiom's Lean formalization of the 246 result (17 Aug 2026) formalizes an existing human proof, so under §5.4 I have left its AxiomProver involvement out of ai.systems. For AI involvement specific to this bullet, I searched explicitly (AI search terms with cousin primes and twin primes, the AI-proof releases, and the Breakthrough Tracker and Erdős coverage) and found no source naming an AI system in connection with the gap-4 question, so the cousin-specific events have ai.none_found true. Close calls: (a) whether the general-Polignac claims count as bearing on the bullet (I recorded them as events because n = 4 is the bullet itself); (b) whether the bounded-gap results count as progress on this bullet (I judge not); (c) I corrected a search summary that said Polymath's conditional H₁ ≤ 6 gives 'gap 6' infinitely often; it only gives one of 2, 4 or 6, so it does not single out 4 either.
competing_reading: Read one of the general-Polignac claims as a resolution. Polignac for every even gap includes n = 4, so Lynch (Jan 2026), the June 2026 Zenodo proof, the MUSTIC paper, Jankovic (2019) or Mothebe et al. (2019), if valid, would settle the bullet, and the problem would then count as resolved from its first posting. Against that: none has been checked by anyone I could find; Lynch's own page gives gap 4 only computational support; the MUSTIC abstract contradicts itself; and the Du and Du and Zafaranich arguments are unread in full or unreadable. A second reading treats the Aug–Sep 2026 bounded-gap papers as progress on this bullet because they move the 'twin/cousin' programme. I do not think that reading holds: H₁ bounds say some gap ≤ c recurs infinitely often, and none of the cited results says which gap that is.
what_would_settle_it: (a) A refereed publication, or an expert write-up in print, that identifies the key step of the Du and Du (2005), Jankovic (2019), Zafaranich and Augusto (2026, restricted), Lynch (2026), June 2026 Zenodo and MUSTIC arguments as valid or invalid. (b) A Lean development with no sorry proving infinitely many p with p+4 prime, or a counterexample to the claim that the sieve lemma of Du and Du holds. (c) A published argument that gives infinitely many occurrences of the specific pattern {0, 4} (for example, a result that the admissible pair {0, 4} has two primes infinitely often). (d) Readable full texts of the PDFs that my tool could not read: Stadlmann (the acknowledgements are not confirmed past the portion I read), Song and Yue (ePrint PDF, 403), OpenAI's paper and axiom list, Charton et al. (bgp212.pdf), the Axiom blueprint, and the Zenodo and MUSTIC PDFs. Any of these would let the later pass check the AI attribution and the method.
